questions.q: Why can a pseudo-random number generator (PRNG) be both 'random-looking' and fully deterministic at the same time?
options: They are not actually deterministic; 'reproducible' PRNGs are a myth
PRNGs secretly use true hardware randomness that happens to be reproducible by coincidence
A PRNG only looks deterministic the first time it is run
A PRNG is a fixed algorithm that, given the same starting seed, always produces the exact same output sequence -- the output just looks statistically unpredictable
questions.explain: A PRNG is a deterministic algorithm -- the same seed and the same sequence of calls always reproduce the same numbers -- which is exactly what makes seeded randomness useful for reproducible science.

questions.q: In the lesson's tiny LCG example, gen_a = tiny_lcg(42) and gen_b = tiny_lcg(42) produced identical sequences [0.582308, 0.519819, 0.91494]. Why?
options: It was a coincidence; different seeds usually also happen to match
The LCG algorithm ignores the seed value entirely
Both generators started from the exact same seed (42) and ran the exact same deterministic update rule, so every step produced an identical value
Because 42 is a special NumPy default value baked into every generator
questions.explain: Identical seed plus identical deterministic algorithm guarantees an identical output sequence -- that's the entire reproducibility guarantee a seed provides, demonstrated by tracing the same multiply-add-mod update from the same starting state.

questions.q: What does a fixed random seed NOT guarantee, according to the lesson?
options: That the exact sequence stays identical forever across different versions of the random-number library if the underlying algorithm changes between versions
That a PRNG is a deterministic algorithm
That two different seeds will usually produce visually different-looking sequences
That the same seed will reproduce the same sequence on the same library version
questions.explain: The lesson notes a seed's guarantee is tied to a specific library version and algorithm -- if the library changes its underlying generator, the exact sequence for a given seed can change, so a research project needing a bit-for-bit historical reproduction should pin its library version.

questions.q: A quantum simulation draws 10,000 samples ('shots') from a distribution where the true probability of outcome '0' is 0.5. According to the law of large numbers reasoning in the lesson, what is the EXACT expected count of '0' outcomes, and is any single run guaranteed to hit that count precisely?
options: The expected count cannot be computed in advance; it is purely a matter of luck
Expected count is 10000, since all shots should return the same outcome
Expected count is exactly 5000 (10000 x 0.5), but no single run is guaranteed to land exactly on it -- only the average over many runs converges toward it
Expected count is exactly 5000, and every single run is guaranteed to produce exactly 5000
questions.explain: N * p = 10000 * 0.5 = 5000 is exact, deterministic arithmetic describing the theoretical average outcome -- it is the right kind of number to sanity-check a simulation against, while acknowledging real statistical noise in any one run.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend `np.random.default_rng(seed)` over the legacy `np.random.seed(seed)` global-state approach for new quantum-simulation code?
options: `default_rng` returns an explicit generator instance you control directly, avoiding hidden global state that other, unrelated parts of a program could silently reset or interfere with
There is no real difference; the recommendation is purely stylistic with no practical benefit
`default_rng` is required because NumPy removed `np.random.seed` entirely
`np.random.seed` does not actually support reproducibility at all
questions.explain: The legacy seed function sets global state that any other code calling NumPy's random functions can also read or reset, which can quietly break reproducibility in a larger program; `default_rng` gives you an isolated generator instance instead.
